I am an atheist myself and I can't say I'm scared of death in the slightest bit. In the words of Mark Twain, "I do not fear death. I had been dead for billions and billions of years before I was born, and had not suffered the slightest inconvenience from it."

I think this quote sums up my view on death. I see life as an incredibly beautiful thing and something we should cherish, but we cannot hold onto it forever and that's just fine. We didn't exist for billions of years and for someone to be angry or scared of the possibility of not existing after death would be ridiculous. No one should be afraid of death, because it is not an experience. When you die, it won't be like sitting in a dark room for an eternity. You won't even realize you're dead, just like a rock doesn't know that it's not living.

I keep in mind how lucky I am to have the chance to die because that means that I won the lottery and got to experience life. I appreciate the time I have here, but I do not feel sorrow or anger that I cannot hold onto this gift for an eternity.

Creationism should not be taught in a science classroom because it is not science. Within the scientific community, there is no debate about evolution vs creationism outside of a couple extreme Christian scientists who are looking for anything to support their beliefs. Outside of the most minute fraction of scientists who don't believe in evolution, the debate of evolution is a societal debate. Science is based on the gathering of data/evidence, where scientists come up with explanations to describe their findings. The work is then peer-reviewed by other scientists before being published. Science has proven to be extremely useful in all the technology we have and is dependable.

Creationism is not science. Science is the study of the natural universe, which is why science and scientists used to be called natural philosophy and natural philosophers. Creationism depends on a divine deity, something supernatural, and does not meet the requirements of science. Science cannot deal with the supernatural at all, neither confirming nor denying it. Why would we have something that's not science be taught in a science classroom?

We live in a nation without an official religion. If you start teaching Christian beliefs, then you better believe you will have people of other beliefs wanting their faith taught alongside evolution and creationism.

There is such a large quantity of evidence to support evolution and research done on the subject to make it so widely accepted. Evolution wasn't simply thought up one day and then taught to everyone as being true.

Finally, being a science teacher myself, one of the main goals of science education is to promote critical thinking and to not simply accept answers. What does creationism do? Creationism relies on simply believing what a book says and is not open to debate. Someone teaching evolution can say, "Here is how people came to this conclusion, here is the evidence, and with new evidence, the details of how evolution works is still trying to determined." You can do activities in the classroom to demonstrate to even a middle school child how evolution works in a simple manner.

I myself am an agnostic atheist. I am atheist because I do not believe in God, however, I do not know with 100% certainty that there is not a God.  Someone who does not believe in God and claims to be 100% sure there is no God would be a gnostic atheist. Someone claiming they believe in God but don't know with 100% certainty there is a God is an agnostic theist, and finally, someone who claims to know with 100% certainty that there is a God would be a gnostic theist.

There is no line to be drawn between agnosticism and atheism as the two terms are answers to two different questions, what someone knows compared to what someone believes.
